positions/midtribulation-rapture/oneLine: The Church will be raptured halfway through the seven-year tribulation, before the great wrath of its last three and a half years.
positions/midtribulation-rapture/coreCla: Daniel’s seventieth week divides into two halves (Dan 9:27; "time, times and half a time"); only the second half is the "great tribulation" of divine wrath.
The "last trump" of 1 Cor 15:52 is the seventh trumpet of Revelation 11:15, sounded at the midpoint.
The two witnesses’ ascension (Rev 11:12) pictures the Church’s rapture.
Believers will see the Antichrist’s rise but be spared God’s wrath.
positions/midtribulation-rapture/origin: A 20th-century variant within premillennialism, articulated by Norman B. Harrison (The End: Re-Thinking the Revelation, 1941), J. Oliver Buswell and Gleason Archer (in Three Views on the Rapture, 1984).
positions/midtribulation-rapture/stronge: Takes seriously the repeated scriptural emphasis on the midpoint of the "week" (42 months, 1,260 days).
Identifies the "last trump" with the last trumpet of Revelation, rather than positing an unmentioned trumpet.
Reconciles texts promising protection from wrath with texts warning believers they will see the Antichrist (2 Thess 2).
The seventh trumpet of Revelation 11 is a judgement trumpet in a symbolic sequence, not obviously Paul’s resurrection trumpet.
Equates the whole second half with "wrath" while texts such as Revelation 6:16–17 announce wrath earlier.
It shares the novelty objection faced by pretribulationism and has very few adherents or institutions.
positions/midtribulation-rapture/respons: Midtribulationists reply that its novelty is no greater than that of any rapture timing and that it best fits the structure of Revelation.
They argue that the sixth-seal declaration of wrath (Rev 6:17) is anticipatory, not the start of its outpouring.
positions/midtribulation-rapture/consequ: Remains a small minority view, mostly of interest in academic debates over rapture timing.
Helped pave the way for the later pre-wrath position.
positions/posttribulation-rapture/oneLin: The Church will go through the final tribulation; the "rapture" is simply believers rising to meet Christ at his one, visible second coming.
positions/posttribulation-rapture/coreCl: There is one future coming of Christ; the gathering of the elect "after the tribulation of those days" (Matt 24:29–31) is the rapture.
Believers are protected from God’s wrath, not removed from persecution; Christians have always suffered tribulation (John 16:33; Acts 14:22).
The "last trump" and the resurrection of the righteous occur at the end of the tribulation (1 Cor 15:52; Rev 20:4).
Those caught up "meet" the Lord to escort him back to earth.
positions/posttribulation-rapture/origin: The default assumption of almost all pre-modern premillennialists (and, in the sense of one coming after tribulation, of amillennialists and postmillennialists). Defended against Darby by Brethren scholars B. W. Newton and S. P. Tregelles, and in the 20th century by Alexander Reese (1937), George Ladd (The Blessed Hope, 1956), Robert Gundry (The Church and the Tribulation, 1973) and Douglas Moo.
positions/posttribulation-rapture/propon: Many Chinese and other persecuted churches
positions/posttribulation-rapture/strong: Matthew 24:29–31 places the gathering of the elect explicitly "after the tribulation", the plainest timing statement in Scripture.
It has the strongest historical pedigree among premillennial options (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.25–30, expected the Church to face Antichrist).
It fits the pattern of 2 Thessalonians 2, where the gathering to Christ follows the man of sin’s revelation.
It prepares believers for suffering rather than promising escape, which many persecuted Christians find more realistic.
Pretribulationists say it destroys imminence: if the tribulation must come first, Christ cannot come "at any moment".
If all believers are glorified at the end of the tribulation, it is unclear who enters the millennium in mortal bodies (for premillennial posttribulationists).
It must explain promises such as Revelation 3:10 ("I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation").
positions/posttribulation-rapture/respon: Posttribulationists reply that New Testament "imminence" means expectancy and readiness, not that no prior events could occur (Peter was told how he would die, John 21:18–19).
Mortal survivors who are converted at Christ’s appearing (e.g. a remnant of Israel, Zech 12:10) could populate the millennium.
"Keep from" (tēreō ek) in John 17:15 means protection within, not removal ("not that thou shouldest take them out of the world").
positions/posttribulation-rapture/conseq: Shapes a theology of perseverance under persecution, influential among underground churches in China and elsewhere.
Provides the main evangelical scholarly alternative to dispensational pretribulationism.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/oneLine: The Church will endure the Antichrist’s persecution in the second half of the seventieth week but be raptured before the "day of the Lord’s wrath", signalled by cosmic signs at the sixth seal.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/coreClaims/0: The "great tribulation" (Antichrist’s persecution of God’s people) and the "day of the Lord" (God’s wrath) are distinct.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/coreClaims/1: The cosmic disturbances of Matthew 24:29 and Revelation 6:12–17 precede both the rapture and the day of the Lord (Joel 2:31).
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/coreClaims/2: The rapture occurs at an unknown time after the midpoint but before the trumpet and bowl judgements.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/coreClaims/3: Believers are exempt from God’s wrath, not from human persecution.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/origin: Formulated by the businessman Robert Van Kampen and popularised by Marvin Rosenthal, a former director of a dispensational mission to Jews, in The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990); developed by Van Kampen’s The Sign (1992) and later by Alan Kurschner and Alan Hultberg.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/strongestArg: Follows the sequence of the Olivet Discourse closely: tribulation, cosmic signs, then the gathering of the elect (Matt 24:29–31).
Joel 2:31 explicitly places the cosmic signs before "the great and terrible day of the LORD", matching the sixth seal and its declaration that the day of wrath "is come" (Rev 6:17).
Reconciles the promise of deliverance from wrath (1 Thess 5:9) with the many warnings that believers will face the Antichrist.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/strongestObj: Pretribulationists object that it, too, abandons imminence and treats the whole seventieth week as not divine wrath, though the seals are opened by the Lamb.
Posttribulationists object that it multiplies distinctions (great tribulation vs day of the Lord) the text does not clearly make.
It is very recent, with a small following and few scholarly defenders.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/responses/0: Advocates reply that the seals are opened by the Lamb but the first five describe human and satanic activity, with wrath announced only at the sixth.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/responses/1: They argue its novelty is a matter of systematisation; the sequence itself is simply that of Matthew 24.
positions/pre-wrath-rapture/consequences: A growing minority view in North American evangelical prophecy circles, especially among former dispensationalists.
Sharpened scholarly debate on the structure of Revelation and the term "day of the Lord".
positions/full-preterism/oneLine: All biblical prophecy, including the second coming, the resurrection and the last judgement, was fulfilled in the events surrounding the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.
positions/full-preterism/coreClaims/0: Jesus promised to return within "this generation" (Matt 24:34; 16:28), and he did, in judgement on Jerusalem in AD 70.
positions/full-preterism/coreClaims/1: The "resurrection" was a corporate, spiritual transition from the old covenant age to the new, completed in AD 70.
positions/full-preterism/coreClaims/2: We now live in the eternal new-covenant age (the "new heavens and new earth"), which has no end.
positions/full-preterism/coreClaims/3: Time-statements ("at hand", "soon", "quickly") must be taken at face value.
positions/full-preterism/origin: Anticipated by J. Stuart Russell’s The Parousia (1878) and Milton Terry; developed as a distinct system by Max R. King (The Spirit of Prophecy, 1971; The Cross and the Parousia, 1987), from a Churches of Christ background, and later by Don Preston and Edward Stevens.
positions/full-preterism/strongestArgume: It takes Jesus’ time-statements with complete seriousness without accusing him of error (against Schweitzer) or stretching "this generation".
The destruction of the Temple was indeed a cosmic-scale event for first-century Jews, matching apocalyptic language elsewhere used for the fall of nations (Isa 13; 34).
It offers a single consistent interpretive key rather than splitting prophecies between past and future.
positions/full-preterism/strongestObject: Every historic creed (Apostles’, Nicene) confesses a future bodily return of Christ "to judge the living and the dead" and "the resurrection of the body"; all major churches regard full preterism as outside orthodoxy.
Paul condemned those who said "the resurrection is past already" (2 Tim 2:17–18).
The resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15 is bodily and coincides with the defeat of death itself, which plainly still reigns.
Acts 1:11 promises Christ will return "in like manner" as he ascended, visibly and bodily.
positions/full-preterism/responses/0: Full preterists reply that the creeds are fallible human documents and that 2 Timothy 2:18 was written before AD 70, when the resurrection was indeed not yet past.
positions/full-preterism/responses/1: They read 1 Corinthians 15 as the raising of the corporate "body" of God’s people out of the old covenant "death".
positions/full-preterism/responses/2: Partial preterists, who share their reading of Matthew 24, remain their strongest critics.
positions/full-preterism/consequences/0: A small, mostly online movement, regarded by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant bodies alike as heterodox.
positions/full-preterism/consequences/1: Has pushed partial preterists to clarify which prophecies remain future.
positions/partial-preterism/oneLine: Much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation (the "great tribulation", the "abomination of desolation", the beast) was fulfilled in the first century, especially the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, while Christ’s bodily return, the resurrection and the judgement remain future.
positions/partial-preterism/coreClaims/0: Jesus’ statement that "this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled" (Matt 24:34) refers to the destruction of the Temple within forty years.
positions/partial-preterism/coreClaims/1: "Coming on the clouds" language in Matthew 24:30 echoes Daniel 7 and Old Testament judgement oracles: vindication and judgement, not necessarily the final return.
positions/partial-preterism/coreClaims/2: Revelation was written before AD 70 (many argue) and mainly addresses the persecuting powers of the first century (Nero as the beast, 666 as "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters).
positions/partial-preterism/coreClaims/3: A future, personal, bodily second coming and general resurrection are distinct and still to come (Acts 1:11; 1 Cor 15).
positions/partial-preterism/origin: Elements in Eusebius and John Chrysostom, who saw Matthew 24 largely fulfilled in AD 70. Systematised by the Spanish Jesuit Luis de Alcázar (Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi, 1614) partly to answer Protestant historicist identification of the pope as Antichrist; adopted by Hugo Grotius (1644) and later by many critical scholars. Popular among Reformed postmillennialists (Kenneth Gentry, R. C. Sproul, Gary DeMar) and, for the Olivet Discourse, among scholars such as N. T. Wright and R. T. France.
positions/partial-preterism/proponentsOt: R. C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus, 1998)
positions/partial-preterism/strongestArg: It honours the plain time-indicators of the Gospels and Revelation ("this generation", "the time is near") without claiming Jesus was mistaken.
Josephus’ Jewish War documents the siege of Jerusalem with horrors matching the "great tribulation" descriptions.
Revelation, as a letter to seven real first-century churches (Rev 1–3), must have been relevant to its first readers.
Unlike full preterism it retains the creedal future return, resurrection and judgement.
positions/partial-preterism/strongestObj: Futurists argue Matthew 24:21 and 29–31 describe an unparalleled worldwide tribulation and a visible coming that AD 70 did not satisfy.
Most scholars date Revelation c.95 under Domitian (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3), after AD 70, which undermines a Jerusalem-focused reading.
Full preterists argue that partial preterism is inconsistent in where it draws the line between fulfilled and future texts.
positions/partial-preterism/responses/0: Partial preterists answer that apocalyptic language is conventionally hyperbolic and that "all the world" (oikoumenē) can mean the Roman world (Luke 2:1).
positions/partial-preterism/responses/1: A pre-70 date for Revelation is defended from internal evidence (the Temple still standing, Rev 11:1–2; the sixth king "is", 17:10).
positions/partial-preterism/responses/2: The line is drawn by the text itself: Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15 clearly describe events not yet fulfilled.
positions/partial-preterism/consequences: Undercuts date-setting and prophecy-news readings of current events.
Provides an exegetical base for postmillennial optimism and for much mainstream scholarship on Mark 13.
Historically blunted Protestant polemic identifying the papacy with Antichrist.
